label: extrinsic (Allport)
source_text: Allport & Ross (1967), as quoted by three fetchable scholarly sources: "Extrinsic values are always instrumental and utilitarian" (cited there as p. 424) and, at the extrinsic end of the continuum, "those who follow religion for personal ends" (Bulbulia, Osborne & Sibley 2013, PLoS ONE); people high in extrinsic orientation use religion "to provide security and solace, sociability and distraction, status and self-justification" (Allport & Ross 1967, p. 434; Wikipedia, Religious orientation); "the extrinsically motivated individual uses his religion, whereas the intrinsically motivated lives his" (p. 434; Flere et al., Europe's Journal of Psychology). Gloss in Neyrinck et al. 2010 (JSSR): "an extrinsically oriented individual approaches religion in a utilitarian or instrumental fashion: it helps one to attain 'self-centered' ends, such as safety, solace, or sociability. Furthermore, religion is lightly held, oversimplified, not reflected upon".
description_draft: This means using one's religion for what it gets one: security and solace, company and distraction, standing and self-justification; the creed itself is held lightly, a means to those ends.
nearest_existing: extrinsically_motivated (motivation in general, not religion) and transactional; religious is the affiliation this axis sits inside. Not a near-duplicate: the axis is how religion is held, not whether.
notes: The 1967 paper (J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 5(4):432-443) is paywalled and no full-text copy could be fetched (the ACU thesis link returned an HTML stub; the UFJF and Brambilla PDFs quote nothing in English), so source_text is assembled from fragments each quoted verbatim by a fetched source, with the quoting source named; nothing bridging them is invented. Quoting sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3858239 (Bulbulia, Osborne & Sibley 2013), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_orientation, https://distantreader.org/stacks/journals/ejop/ejop-397.htm (Flere, Lavrič, Musil & Klanjšek), https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/2010_NeyrinckLensetal_JSSR.pdf (Neyrinck, Lens, Vansteenkiste & Soenens 2010). The PMC citation's 'p. 424' lies outside the paper's page range and is probably a typo; left as cited. 'held lightly' comes through Neyrinck's gloss (which also cites Allport 1950), not from a fetched 1967 sentence. Strength: the source is pointed ('always instrumental and utilitarian') and the draft matches it; 'self-justification' kept as Allport's word because the plain alternatives ('a good conscience') soften it.
pair_review: The extrinsic draft lists five concrete uses (Allport's own nouns) and ends on how the creed is held; the intrinsic draft is abstract (master motive, other needs fitted around it) and ends on internalizing the creed. Same closing topic, different concreteness: a re-edit could give intrinsic one concrete habit or trim extrinsic's list. Extrinsic also rests on more, shorter fragments than intrinsic. 'uses his religion / lives his religion' is Allport's own antithesis and is deliberately not used in either draft, to avoid naming the partner.

label: Gemeinschaft (Tönnies)
source_text: All kinds of social co-existence that are familiar, comfortable and exclusive are to be understood as belonging to Gemeinschaft. Gesellschaft means life in the public sphere, in the outside world. In Gemeinschaft we are united from the moment of our birth with our own folk for better or for worse. We go out into Gesellschaft as if into a foreign land. [...] human wills, each one housed in a physical body, are related to one another by descent and kinship; they remain united, or become so out of necessity. [...] In Gemeinschaft they stay together in spite of everything that separates them; in Gesellschaft they remain separate in spite of everything that unites them.
description_draft: This means belonging from birth to one's own folk for better or worse, living the familiar, comfortable, exclusive life of kin and home, and staying together in spite of all that separates.
nearest_existing: collectivistic and clannish (group before self; one's own circle), with rooted and family_oriented nearby. Not a near-duplicate: this is a whole way of being bound to people, not a preference.
notes: Tönnies' own words in the Harris & Hollis translation (Community and Civil Society, CUP 2001, pp. 17-19, 22-24, 52-54, 257-58), as excerpted on German History Intersections; the excerpt is what was fetched, not the whole book. The excerpt names kinship, descent, mother and child, husband and wife, siblings and the 'domestic community'; it does not mention neighbourhood or the village, so the draft says 'kin and home' rather than the queue note's 'family, village and faith'. Strength: the source is warm and declarative, and the draft keeps that; no hedges to render.
pair_review: Tönnies' two passages are not equally tempered: Gemeinschaft is described warmly (familiar, comfortable, united for better or worse) and Gesellschaft harshly (out for himself alone, tension against everyone else, gives nothing without an equal trade-off). Under rule 3 both drafts mirror their source, so Gemeinschaft reads as a virtue and Gesellschaft as a vice; that is the source's asymmetry, flagged for Roger rather than evened out. Scope: the Gemeinschaft draft names the institutions (kin, home) while the Gesellschaft draft names none (the fetched passage does not name market, contract or state), which a re-edit could add from the queue notes.

label: Gesellschaft (Tönnies)
source_text: The theory of Gesellschaft takes as its starting point a group of people who, as in Gemeinschaft, live peacefully alongside one another, but in this case without being essentially united – indeed, on the contrary, they are here essentially detached. In Gemeinschaft they stay together in spite of everything that separates them; in Gesellschaft they remain separate in spite of everything that unites them. [...] Nothing happens in Gesellschaft that is more important for the individual's wider group than it is for himself. On the contrary, everyone is out for himself alone and living in a state of tension against everyone else. [...] Nobody wants to do anything for anyone else, nobody wants to yield or give anything unless he gets something in return that he regards as at least an equal trade-off.
description_draft: This means living alongside others without being joined to them, out for oneself alone and in tension with everyone else, and giving nothing away except in exchange for at least as much.
nearest_existing: transactional (relationships weighed by what they yield) and individualistic; calculating and detached nearby. Not a near-duplicate: transactional is a stance toward dealings, this is the person's whole social world.
notes: Same page and translation as the Gemeinschaft entry, section 'The Theory of Gesellschaft'. Strength: the source is harsh ('out for himself alone', 'tension against everyone else', 'nobody wants to do anything for anyone else') and the draft keeps it at that pitch rather than softening toward 'impersonal' or 'businesslike'; 'live peacefully alongside one another' is rendered as 'living alongside others' (the peacefulness dropped only for length; it qualifies the tension, so a re-edit might restore it). Markedly harsher than the corpus's transactional; noted as the source's doing.

label: high-context (Hall)
source_text: "A high-context (HC) communication or message is one in which most of the information is either in the physical context or internalized in the person, while very little is in the coded, explicit, transmitted part of the message" (Hall 1976, p. 91). As described by Hall, high-context communication is characteristic of cultures in which people are "deeply involved" with one another and information is widely shared among them (Hall 1976, 39). [...] "When talking about something they have on their minds, a high-context individual will expect others to know what's bothering him, so that he doesn't have to be specific" (Hall 1976, 113).
description_draft: This means letting the setting and shared history carry most of one's meaning, putting very little into the words themselves, and expecting others to know what is bothering one without being told.
nearest_existing: cryptic and enigmatic (meaning withheld from the words), with tactful, understated and figurative nearby. Not a near-duplicate: the test is where the meaning sits (setting and shared knowledge), not whether the speaker is being obscure or polite.
notes: Hall's own definition from Beyond Culture (1976) as quoted with page numbers in Chris Oliver, 'From Class to Culture: Restricted/Elaborated Codes vs. High/Low-context Communication in Basil Bernstein and Edward T. Hall', Sophia University Junior College Division Faculty Journal 37 (2016), 73-83. Wikipedia's article paraphrases Hall but does not quote him; a second handout (https://support.wspa.pl/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/02_Text_Topic-3.2_Cultural-Dimensions-by-E.-T.-Hall.pdf) quotes a variant of the same definition ('already in the person', cited to p. 101) with Hall's twins-versus-lawyers example. Strength: Hall is categorical ('most', 'very little') and the draft keeps those words; 'will expect others to know' rendered as 'expecting others to know'.
pair_review: The high-context draft ends with Hall's sentence about an individual (expects others to know what is bothering him, p. 113); the low-context draft ends with an assumption ('taking for granted that others share little of one's background') built from Hall's remarks about low-context cultures (p. 39: 'highly individualized, somewhat alienated, fragmented') and about encoding (p. 101), not from a sentence about an individual. The two closing clauses therefore rest on unequal sources. The high side also names 'shared history' where the low side mentions only the setting. 'somewhat alienated' was not carried into the low-context draft; a re-edit could render it.

label: intrinsic (Allport)
source_text: Allport & Ross (1967), as quoted by fetchable scholarly sources: at the intrinsic end are those who "find their master motive in religion" (p. 434; Bulbulia, Osborne & Sibley 2013, PLoS ONE); "Having embraced a creed the individual endeavours to internalize it and follow it fully. It is in this sense that he lives his religion" (p. 434; Tønnesvang 2003, Psyke & Logos). Gloss in Neyrinck et al. 2010 (JSSR): "An intrinsically oriented person considers religion as an ultimate end in itself; it is a master motive in life. Religious beliefs and values (e.g., humility, compassion, etc.) are internalized 'without reservation,' and other needs and goals are accommodated, reorganized, and brought in harmony with these religious contents. Importantly, an intrinsic religious orientation 'floods the whole life with motivation and meaning' (Allport 1966:455)."
description_draft: This means making religion the master motive of one's life, fitting one's other needs around it, and, having taken up a creed, striving to make it one's own and follow it fully.
nearest_existing: religious (belief and practice) and intrinsically_motivated (motivation in general); zealous and orthodox are neighbours of a different kind (fervour; which doctrine). Not a near-duplicate: religious says that one believes, this says religion is the end everything else serves.
notes: Same fetch problem as the extrinsic entry: the 1967 paper could not be fetched, so the text is fragments quoted verbatim by the named sources. Quoting sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3858239, https://tidsskrift.dk/psyke/article/download/8652/7225/27413 (Jan Tønnesvang, 'Religiøsitetens selvobjektfunktionalitet & tilknytningsdimensioner', Psyke & Logos 24 (2003), 778-805, which quotes the English with British spelling 'endeavours'), https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/2010_NeyrinckLensetal_JSSR.pdf. 'Other needs, strong as they may be, are regarded as of less ultimate significance' (the usual continuation) was not found verbatim on any fetched page and is not in source_text; 'fitting one's other needs around it' renders Neyrinck's gloss of it. Strength: the source is strong and unhedged ('master motive', 'follow it fully') and so is the draft.

label: loose (Gelfand)
source_text: With data from 33 nations, we illustrate the differences between cultures that are tight (have many strong norms and a low tolerance of deviant behavior) versus loose (have weak social norms and a high tolerance of deviant behavior). Tightness-looseness is part of a complex, loosely integrated multilevel system that comprises distal ecological and historical threats (e.g., high population density, resource scarcity, a history of territorial conflict, and disease and environmental threats), broad versus narrow socialization in societal institutions (e.g., autocracy, media regulations), the strength of everyday recurring situations, and micro-level psychological affordances (e.g., prevention self-guides, high regulatory strength, need for structure).
description_draft: This means holding only weak rules of conduct, leaving people to decide for themselves how to behave in most situations, and putting up readily with behavior that steps well outside the usual.
nearest_existing: permissive and lenient (what one lets others get away with), with easygoing and laid_back nearby. Not a near-duplicate: permissive is about one's own allowing; this is how strong one expects the rules to be at all.
notes: Abstract of Gelfand et al., 'Differences between tight and loose cultures: a 33-nation study', Science 332 (2011), 1100-1104 (doi 10.1126/science.1197754), fetched through Europe PMC's REST API; PubMed (cookie wall) and europepmc.org's HTML page (HTTP 403) could not be fetched, and science.org was not tried. Gelfand's lab site (michelegelfand.com) has no definitional text beyond 'more restrictive or permissive norms'. The abstract's definition of each pole is one parenthesis, so the drafts are thin by construction; the loose draft's middle clause renders 'broad socialization' and weak 'everyday recurring situations' as a person's habit. Strength: the source is a flat comparative ('weak', 'high tolerance'); 'only weak' and 'readily' carry that, no sharpening.
pair_review: Both drafts come from the same two parentheses, so scope matches on the first and third clauses (strength of rules; tolerance of deviance). The middle clauses differ in origin: tight's 'wanting structure and self-restraint' renders the abstract's micro-level affordances (need for structure, prevention self-guides, regulatory strength), which have no loose-side counterpart in the text; loose's 'leaving people to decide for themselves' renders 'broad socialization', which has no tight-side clause. The tight self-restraint clause also brushes against the queue note's warning that this axis is norm enforcement in others, not one's own compliance (conformist); Roger may want it cut or reworded toward sanctioning others.

label: low-context (Hall)
source_text: "A low-context (LC) communication is just the opposite; i.e., the mass of the information is vested in the explicit code" (Hall 1976, p. 91). [...] low-context communication is said by Hall to be characteristic of "highly individualized, somewhat alienated, fragmented cultures" (Hall 1976, 39). Thus, whereas high-context messages can be verbally abbreviated and compact, low-context messages involve a greater use of explicit code to provide the conveyance of meaning. Precisely because there is less "pre-programmed" information shared between participants in low-context communication, most of the information "must be [encoded] in the transmitted message in order to make up for what is missing in the context" (Hall 1976, 101).
description_draft: This means putting the mass of one's meaning into the explicit words, spelling out whatever the setting does not supply, and taking for granted that others share little of one's background.
nearest_existing: plain_spoken and literal (meaning in the words as said), with blunt, forthright and clear nearby. Not a near-duplicate: plain_spoken is about manner; this is about where the information is put, whatever the manner.
notes: Same source as high-context (Oliver 2016 quoting Hall 1976, pp. 91, 39, 101); the second and third sentences of source_text are Oliver's connecting prose around Hall's quoted phrases, kept so the quoted fragments are not isolated. Strength: Hall's 'the mass of the information' is kept as 'the mass of one's meaning'; the clause about others sharing little background renders 'highly individualized ... fragmented' and 'what is missing in the context' without the hedge 'somewhat', which is flagged in the pair review.

label: monochronic (Hall)
source_text: M-time, on the other hand, is oriented to tasks, schedules, and procedures. As anyone who has had experience with our bureaucracies knows, schedules and procedures take on a life all their own without reference to either logic or human needs. ...M-time is also tangible; we speak of it as being saved, spent, wasted, lost, made up, crawling, killed, and running out (pp. 43, 50). [Hall & Hall 1990, p. 15, monochronic actions:] Do one thing at a time; Concentrate on the job; Take time schedules seriously; Are low context and need information; Are committed to the job; Adhere strictly to plans; Are concerned about not disturbing others and follow rules of privacy; Show great respect for private property; rarely borrow or lend; Emphasize promptness; Are accustomed to short-term relationships.
description_draft: This means doing one thing at a time, organizing life around tasks, schedules and procedures, treating time as a thing to be saved, spent, wasted or lost, and keeping to the clock.
nearest_existing: methodical (one step at a time, in order) and organized; focused, efficient and hurried nearby. Not a near-duplicate: methodical is about how a task is done, this is about how time itself is held (segmented, scheduled, tangible).
notes: Hall's own words from The Dance of Life (1983), pp. 43 and 50, as quoted on Michael Kearl's Trinity University page 'The Times of Our Lives: Cultural Rhythms' (the first part of source_text, verbatim including the page's ellipses). The bracketed list is Hall & Hall, Understanding Cultural Differences (1990), p. 15, as reproduced in the WSPA handout https://support.wspa.pl/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/02_Text_Topic-3.2_Cultural-Dimensions-by-E.-T.-Hall.pdf ('adapted from Hall and Hall'); it supplies 'one thing at a time' and promptness, which the 1983 passage states only for P-time by contrast. Hall's aside that M-time schedules 'take on a life all their own without reference to either logic or human needs' is about bureaucracies and was not turned into a habit of the person; a re-edit could add it ('even when they serve no one'), which would make the pole harsher. Strength: as the source, matter-of-fact, no hedges.
pair_review: The polychronic draft is entirely from the 1983 passage; the monochronic draft needed the 1990 table for 'one thing at a time' and 'keeping to the clock' because Hall's M-time paragraph is shorter and partly an aside. Scope differs in one place: polychronic ends with 'hearing people out, schedule or no schedule' (Hall's 'cannot cut them off simply because of a schedule'), to which the M-time text gives no counterpart, and monochronic's 'tangible time' clause has a P-time counterpart ('seldom feeling that time is wasted') that is present. Tone: Hall writes P-time warmly ('if you value people') and M-time drily ('bureaucracies'); the drafts carry a trace of that.

label: polychronic (Hall)
source_text: P-time stresses involvement of people and completion of transactions rather than adherence to preset schedules. ... For polychronic people, time is seldom experienced as "wasted," and is apt to be considered a point rather than a ribbon or a road, but that point is often sacred. ...Polychronic cultures are by their very nature oriented to people. Any human being who is naturally drawn to other human beings and who lives in a world dominated by human relationships will be either pushed or pulled toward the polychronic end of the time spectrum. If you value people, you must hear them out and cannot cut them off simply because of a schedule.
description_draft: This means doing many things at once, putting people and the business at hand before a preset schedule, seldom feeling that time is wasted, and hearing people out, schedule or no schedule.
nearest_existing: improvisational (plans changed as one goes) and distractible; unhurried, spontaneous and other_focused nearby. Not a near-duplicate: improvisational is about method; this is about several things and several people held at once, with the schedule yielding to them.
notes: Hall's own words, The Dance of Life (1983), pp. 43 and 50, as quoted on the Trinity page (verbatim, with the page's ellipses). 'Doing many things at once' is from the Hall & Hall 1990 table ('Do many things at once'; see the monochronic entry's notes), since the 1983 passage names involvement and completion rather than simultaneity. Strength: 'seldom' kept as 'seldom'; 'you must hear them out and cannot cut them off' rendered as 'hearing people out, schedule or no schedule', the same strength in plain words; 'often sacred' not carried (length).

label: secular-rational (Inglehart-Welzel)
source_text: Secular-rational values have the opposite preferences to the traditional values. These societies place less emphasis on religion, traditional family values and authority. Divorce, abortion, euthanasia and suicide are seen as relatively acceptable. (Suicide is not necessarily more common.)
description_draft: This means setting less store by religion, the family and authority than others do, and seeing divorce, abortion, euthanasia and suicide as fairly acceptable.
nearest_existing: secular (one's own religiosity) and progressive; rationalist by name only. Not a deliberate duplicate: the scope here is the WVS cluster (religion plus family, authority and the four life-and-death questions), not religiosity alone.
notes: World Values Survey, 'Findings and Insights' (Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map section), the WVS's own description of the dimension; the page credits Inglehart & Welzel 2005, Modernization, Cultural Change and Democracy, ch. 2. Strength: the source defines this pole only comparatively ('less emphasis', 'relatively acceptable'), so the draft keeps the comparative ('less ... than others do') and renders 'relatively' as 'fairly'. This pole therefore comes out markedly milder than the corpus's plain traits (secular, progressive): it asserts no positive commitment, only less of the traditional ones. Flagged under rule 3 for Roger. 'traditional family values' is rendered 'the family' so the description does not echo the partner label.
pair_review: The traditional pole is stated as positive commitments (religion, family, deference, the four rejections, national pride); the secular-rational pole is stated as comparatives ('less emphasis', 'relatively acceptable') and the WVS adds 'the opposite preferences'. The drafts mirror this, so one reads as a creed and the other as its absence-by-degree; that is the source's framing, flagged, not fixed. Scope: traditional carries national pride and a 'nationalistic outlook' with no secular-rational counterpart in the source, and 'parent-child ties' becomes 'keeping parents and children close' on the traditional side only.

label: self-expression (Inglehart-Welzel)
source_text: Self-expression values give high priority to environmental protection, growing tolerance of foreigners, gays and lesbians and gender equality, and rising demands for participation in decision-making in economic and political life.
description_draft: This means giving high priority to protecting the environment, accepting foreigners, gays and lesbians, treating women and men as equals, and demanding a say in economic and political decisions.
nearest_existing: progressive (the nearest single trait), with environmental, inclusive, egalitarian, feminist, gay_affirming and pro_immigration each covering one clause. Not a deliberate duplicate: this bundles four commitments the corpus holds separately, as the instrument does.
notes: Same WVS page as the other Inglehart-Welzel entries. Strength: 'high priority' kept; 'growing tolerance' rendered 'accepting' (tolerance is the source's word, and 'welcoming' would sharpen it); 'rising demands for participation' rendered 'demanding a say'. No hedges in the source and none in the draft. The queue note treats postmaterialism as identical to this pole; the WVS text does not use the word, so nothing was added for it.
pair_review: The two sources are not mirror images: self-expression lists four commitments (environment, tolerance of foreigners and gays and lesbians, gender equality, participation); survival has three (economic and physical security, an ethnocentric outlook, low trust and tolerance), and only tolerance appears on both sides. The survival draft also carries two hedges ('somewhat', 'little') where the self-expression draft has none, because the WVS writes 'relatively ethnocentric' and 'low levels'; survival thus reads milder and vaguer than self-expression. A re-edit could not add security to self-expression or the environment to survival without going beyond the source.

label: survival (Inglehart-Welzel)
source_text: Survival values place emphasis on economic and physical security. It is linked with a relatively ethnocentric outlook and low levels of trust and tolerance.
description_draft: This means caring first about economic and physical security, measuring other peoples somewhat by one's own, and extending little trust or tolerance to others.
nearest_existing: ethnocentric and guarded, with insular, risk_averse and loss_averse nearby. Not a deliberate duplicate: ethnocentric is one clause of this; the core is security first.
notes: Same WVS page. Strength: 'place emphasis on' rendered 'caring first about' (emphasis, not 'above all else'); 'relatively ethnocentric' rendered 'measuring other peoples somewhat by one's own' with the hedge kept as 'somewhat'; 'low levels of trust and tolerance' rendered 'little trust or tolerance'. The source is the shortest of the fourteen (two sentences, 24 words) and the mildest in wording, so this pole comes out milder than the corpus's plain ethnocentric or insular; flagged under rule 3. 'Economic and physical security' kept as the recognisable canonical phrase rather than a plainer 'making a living and staying safe'.

label: tight (Gelfand)
source_text: With data from 33 nations, we illustrate the differences between cultures that are tight (have many strong norms and a low tolerance of deviant behavior) versus loose (have weak social norms and a high tolerance of deviant behavior). Tightness-looseness is part of a complex, loosely integrated multilevel system that comprises distal ecological and historical threats (e.g., high population density, resource scarcity, a history of territorial conflict, and disease and environmental threats), broad versus narrow socialization in societal institutions (e.g., autocracy, media regulations), the strength of everyday recurring situations, and micro-level psychological affordances (e.g., prevention self-guides, high regulatory strength, need for structure).
description_draft: This means holding many strong rules of conduct, expecting them to apply in nearly every situation, having little tolerance for anyone who steps outside them, and wanting structure and self-restraint.
nearest_existing: strict and judgmental (rules for others, enforced), with rule_abiding, conformist, conventional and uptight nearby. Not a deliberate duplicate: the queue note's test is norm enforcement in others, distinct from conformist (own compliance) and from formal rules.
notes: Same abstract as the loose entry (Gelfand et al. 2011, Science; via Europe PMC's REST API). The pole's definition in the source is one parenthesis ('many strong norms and a low tolerance of deviant behavior'); 'expecting them to apply in nearly every situation' renders 'the strength of everyday recurring situations', and 'wanting structure and self-restraint' renders the micro-level affordances (need for structure, prevention self-guides, high regulatory strength), which the abstract lists for the tight side of the system. Strength: 'many strong', 'low tolerance' kept as 'many strong', 'little tolerance'; no sharpening toward punishment, which the abstract does not mention. See the pair review on the loose entry for the self-restraint clause.

label: traditional (Inglehart-Welzel)
source_text: Traditional values emphasize the importance of religion, parent-child ties, deference to authority and traditional family values. People who embrace these values also reject divorce, abortion, euthanasia and suicide. These societies have high levels of national pride and a nationalistic outlook.
description_draft: This means putting religion, the family and deference to authority first, keeping parents and children close, rejecting divorce, abortion, euthanasia and suicide, and taking great pride in one's nation.
nearest_existing: conservative and traditional (the plain trait, paired with innovative, is about custom versus novelty), with religious, family_oriented, nationalist and orthodox each covering one clause. Not a deliberate duplicate: the suffix marks the WVS scope, which bundles religion, family, authority, the four rejections and national pride.
notes: Same WVS page. Strength: the source is declarative ('emphasize', 'reject', 'high levels of national pride') and the draft matches it, with 'deference to authority' kept as the source's word (plainer 'respect for' would soften it). 'A nationalistic outlook' is folded into 'taking great pride in one's nation'; a re-edit wanting the outlook as well as the pride would need a few more words. Not milder than the corpus's plain traits.
